beginner.headline: Museum Thefts Are Becoming Bolder in Europe
beginner.brief: Museum thefts are becoming bolder in Europe. Thieves recently stole four paintings from a French museum. These paintings were by artist Renoir. They were worth millions of euros. Museums are often in old buildings, so they are hard to protect. Experts say museums need more time to stop thieves. Some museums are adding more security, like enhanced video surveillance.

intermediate.headline: Museum Thefts Across Europe Become Bolder and More Frequent
intermediate.brief: Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen. When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, not everyone was surprised. The European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen just last month. Internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted that more high-profile burglaries were likely after a successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris. The audacious crime at the Louvre stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m has still not been recovered. Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks. Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition. Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up. Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report. Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process. Christopher A Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered. Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive or deter would-be offenders. However, security measures are expensive, and finding the money is a main challenge for smaller cities with important collections. A museum cannot be a fortress, but institutions are facing new challenges that will require new security standards.

advanced.headline: Europe's Museums Under Siege: The Rise of Bold Art Heists
advanced.brief: Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen. When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised. Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen. Internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely, particularly after the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October. The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on. Brand believes that the Louvre's successful breach signalled to thieves globally that local museums with valuable items might also be targeted. Europol indicates that the number of reported museum theft cases across Europe began to increase approximately two years ago. Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing, with a rise in more forceful tactics and a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones. The Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA) says the recent thefts show a repeated preference for small, portable, immediately accessible objects and for attacks designed to be completed in minutes. These crimes threaten what many consider invaluable artefacts of historical and cultural value enjoyed by the public. Brand argues that museums are inherently vulnerable compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks. Directors historically 'never have enough money for security' or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect. Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control, allowing perpetrators to come in as visitors. Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up; the Renoir case happened within five minutes. Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, with offenders using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars, and even explosives. Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process. Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it. Security is about buying time, making removal difficult, noisy, detectable and, above all, time-consuming, because thefts can always happen. Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems, so for example, if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility or lock down all high net worth paintings. Mayor Caviezel says finding the money for security measures is 'one of our main challenges' for a small city entrusted with national collections. It could also involve training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum, which may deter them from returning. Ultimately, a museum cannot be a fortress; it must balance openness with new standards for facing challenges and attacks.
